incidents.name: SushiSwap RouteProcessor2 unvalidated route pool
incidents.notes: RouteProcessor2.processRoute() never checked that the pool address encoded in the user-supplied `route` was a real UniswapV3 pool, so an attacker-controlled 'pool' could call back into uniswapV3SwapCallback and make the router execute transferFrom against any wallet that had approved it.

sources.ref: onchain review: RouteProcessor2 0x044b75f554b886a065b9567891e45c79542d7357 created 2023-04-05 by 0xf87bc5535602077d340806d71f805ea9907a843d (Sushi deployer), unrelated to the attack senders; no EIP-1967 Upgraded events, so the exploited code was 3.8 days old. The flaw was exploited by many independent senders in blocks 17007838-17007844 draining approvals from 0x31d3243cfb54b34fc9c73e1cb1137124bd6b13e1; the tx recorded here is the 800 WETH drain named in Sushi's own post-mortem, sent by the MEV searcher c0ffeebabe.eth which returned funds, while other replays (e.g. 0x8ac0b9656b7c39be0d3d73828d2041e8c0e27712) kept them
